title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia: 4Ts, PF4 Assays and the Switch
summary: Learn how PF4/heparin antibodies cause clotting, how the 4Ts score decides who gets tested, why a sensitive PF4 immunoassay needs a functional assay to confirm, and how to manage HIT: stop all heparin, avoid LMWH, and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 39 Hit 2 (stop all heparin/LMWH; non-heparin anticoagulant; 4Ts), Hit 11 (immunoassay vs functional assay), Hit 12 (argatroban/bivalirudin half-lives, APTT target), Trap 4 (LMWH in HIT) and the argatroban–INR part of Hit 5. Checked against the ASH 2018 HIT guideline (Cuker 2018; read via a page-fetch tool), Warkentin and Greinacher 2023, Marchetti 2021 and Patriarcheas 2020. Corrections: Hit 2’s “low 4T score = 0–3% HIT probability” conflates the 0–3-point range with a probability (register flag rv-hit-4t-low-points); Hit 11’s specificity figure is assay- and threshold-dependent (rv-hit-eia-specificity); fondaparinux “does not cross-react in vivo” is given more cautiously by sources (rv-hit-fondaparinux-context). Pending: Hit 5’s heparin neutralisation to isolate the warfarin effect; Hit 11’s EIA excess-heparin confirmatory step; the exact 98.1/89.4% figures; Hit 12’s heparin-resistance figure (>35,000 U/day).

objectives: Explain how PF4/heparin IgG immune complexes activate platelets and cause thrombosis, and state the typical timing of HIT.
Use the 4Ts score to decide who should have HIT laboratory testing, and interpret PF4 immunoassay and functional assay results.
Outline acute HIT management: stop all heparin, avoid LMWH, choose a non-heparin anticoagulant, and delay warfarin until platelet recovery.

scenes.title: Day 7 on heparin
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a post-operative patient on unfractionated heparin (UFH). Platelet count 250 ×10⁹/L before surgery, 95 ×10⁹/L on day 7 (a 62% fall); a new deep-vein thrombosis appears the same day. A ward note suggests: “switch to enoxaparin, it is a different heparin.” Question token: “HIT? And is LMWH safe?”

cues.text: Invented case: a patient on unfractionated heparin after surgery. The platelet count falls from two hundred fifty to ninety-five on day seven.
On the same day a new deep-vein clot appears. Someone suggests switching to enoxaparin, because it is a different heparin.
Is this heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and is the low-molecular-weight heparin safe?

scenes.title: Why heparin can cause clots
scenes.altText: Schematic: cationic platelet factor 4 (PF4) tetramers bound to anionic heparin form complexes that expose new antigen sites. IgG antibodies bind the PF4/heparin complexes; the immune complexes cross-link platelet FcγIIa receptors → strong platelet activation → thrombin generation and thrombosis. Timing card: typical onset 5–10 days after starting heparin; rapid onset (within about a day) if heparin was given in the previous ~100 days. Risk card: UFH carries roughly 10-fold the HIT risk of LMWH; thrombosis is frequent (classic HIT absolute risk about 50–70%).

cues.text: Platelet factor four is a positively charged platelet protein. Heparin is negatively charged, so the two bind, and the complex exposes new antigen sites on platelet factor four.
Some patients make IgG against these complexes. The immune complexes engage platelet Fc gamma two A receptors and strongly activate platelets, so the result is clotting, not bleeding.
The platelet fall typically begins five to ten days after heparin starts. If the patient had heparin within roughly the last hundred days, it can fall within a day.
Unfractionated heparin carries roughly ten times the risk of low-molecular-weight heparin, and thrombosis is common in classic HIT.

scenes.title: 4Ts first, then the right test
scenes.altText: 4Ts card: Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, oTher causes; each 0–2 points, total 0–8. Low 0–3 points: negative predictive value about 99.8% → ASH 2018 recommends against HIT laboratory testing and against empiric HIT treatment (caveat: HIT has been reported with a score of 3). Intermediate 4–5 / high 6–8 points: positive predictive value about 14% and 64%. Testing pathway card: intermediate/high → immunoassay (PF4-dependent EIA; sensitivity >99%, lower specificity); positive → functional (platelet activation) assay such as the serotonin-release assay (SRA) or heparin-induced platelet activation (HIPA) test, which are more specific.

cues.text: Start with the four T’s: thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis, and other causes. Each scores zero to two points, for a total of zero to eight.

A low score is zero to three points, not a percentage. Its negative predictive value is about ninety-nine point eight percent, so the 2018 ASH guideline advises no HIT testing and no empiric HIT treatment. A few cases have been reported with a score of three.
Intermediate scores, four to five, and high scores, six to eight, have positive predictive values of only about fourteen and sixty-four percent. So these patients get an immunoassay.

The PF4 immunoassay is very sensitive, over ninety-nine percent, but less specific. If it is positive, a functional platelet activation assay, such as the serotonin-release assay, is the more specific confirmation.

scenes.title: Managing the hook patient
scenes.altText: Management card (high-probability or confirmed HIT): stop ALL heparin from every source, including flushes and heparin-coated catheters; do not substitute LMWH (HIT antibodies react with it); start a therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor, half-life ~45 min, hepatobiliary clearance, APTT target 1.5–3× baseline), bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitor, half-life ~25 min, proteolytic and renal clearance), danaparoid or fondaparinux (antithrombin-dependent anti-Xa agents), or a DOAC (ASH 2018, conditional). Warfarin card: do not start a vitamin K antagonist until platelets recover (usually ≥150 ×10⁹/L); argatroban itself raises the INR, so the overlap is tricky. No routine platelet transfusion unless bleeding or high bleeding risk.

cues.text: The hook patient has a high-probability picture: a large fall on day seven with a new clot. Stop every heparin source now, including flushes and heparin-coated catheters, without waiting for the test.

Do not switch to low-molecular-weight heparin: HIT antibodies react with it too. Start a non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban, bivalirudin, danaparoid, fondaparinux, or in some cases a direct oral anticoagulant.

Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor with a half-life of about forty-five minutes, cleared by the liver and often adjusted to an APTT of one and a half to three times baseline. Bivalirudin lasts about twenty-five minutes and is cleared by enzymes and the kidneys.

Hold warfarin until the platelet count recovers, and remember argatroban itself raises the INR, which complicates the switch. Platelet transfusion is not routine; it may be considered with bleeding or a high bleeding risk.

props.title: Stop every source
lines: Do not wait for the test

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “LMWH is a different heparin, so it is safe in HIT” (✓ HIT antibodies react with LMWH; use a non-heparin anticoagulant); “A positive PF4 immunoassay confirms HIT” (✓ the EIA is sensitive but less specific; confirm with a functional assay and the clinical picture); “A low 4Ts score means a 0–3% chance” (✓ 0–3 is the point range out of 8 of the low category; its negative predictive value is ~99.8%).

cues.text: Trap one: low-molecular-weight heparin is a different heparin, so it is safe. No: HIT antibodies react with it. Switch to a non-heparin drug.
Trap two: a positive PF4 immunoassay confirms HIT. No: it is sensitive but less specific. Confirm with a functional assay and the clinical picture.
Trap three: reading the low 4Ts band as zero to three percent. Zero to three is the point range, out of eight. The low category has a negative predictive value near ninety-nine point eight percent.

scenes.title: Every drop, the cousin, a stranger
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Stop EVERY DROP (infusions, flushes, coated lines), shun the COUSIN (LMWH), switch to a STRANGER (a non-heparin anticoagulant).” Tokens: every drop · cousin · stranger. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: stop every drop of heparin, including flushes. Shun the cousin, low-molecular-weight heparin. Switch to a stranger, a non-heparin anticoagulant.

Where it breaks: fondaparinux is a heparin-like pentasaccharide yet is a guideline-suggested option, because it only rarely causes HIT; warfarin is a stranger too but must wait for platelet recovery; and a low 4Ts score means you should not test or treat at all.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “4Ts first · low 0–3 points = no test · intermediate/high → EIA → functional assay”, “Stop every heparin source · no LMWH · switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant · warfarin after platelet recovery”.

cues.text: In suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, score the 4Ts first, test only intermediate or high scores with a sensitive immunoassay backed by a more specific functional assay, and treat by stopping every heparin source, including low-molecular-weight heparin, and switching to a non-heparin anticoagulant.

props.label: 4Ts first · low = no test · EIA → functional assay
Stop all heparin · no LMWH · non-heparin drug · VKA later

explanation.what: Plain language: in a few people on heparin, the immune system makes antibodies against a platelet protein stuck to heparin. Those antibodies switch platelets on, so the platelet count drops while dangerous clots form. Doctors first score how likely this is, then test with a sensitive antibody test and, if positive, a more specific platelet test. Treatment is to stop all heparin and use a different kind of blood thinner. Scientific terms: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), platelet factor 4 (PF4), FcγIIa receptor, 4Ts score, negative and positive predictive value, PF4-dependent enzyme immunoassay (EIA), serotonin-release assay (SRA), heparin-induced platelet activation (HIPA) test, direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin), danaparoid, fondaparinux, vitamin K antagonist (VKA).
explanation.why: Heparin binding exposes new antigens on PF4; IgG/PF4/heparin immune complexes cross-link platelet FcγIIa receptors and drive platelet activation and thrombin generation. Many heparin-exposed patients make non-pathogenic anti-PF4 antibodies, which is why immunoassays are sensitive but less specific, and why functional assays that detect platelet activation (and its inhibition by high heparin concentrations) are more specific.
explanation.measure: 4Ts: 4 items, 0–2 each, total 0–8; low 0–3 points (NPV ~99.8%: no testing, no empiric treatment), intermediate 4–5 and high 6–8 (PPV ~14% and ~64%: immunoassay, then functional assay if positive). PF4 EIA sensitivity >99%; washed-platelet functional assays ~95% sensitivity and specificity with careful technique (selected donors, weak-positive controls). Argatroban half-life ~45 min, APTT 1.5–3× baseline; bivalirudin ~25 min. No VKA until platelets recover (usually ≥150 ×10⁹/L).
explanation.differs: Immunoassay (antibody binding, sensitive) vs functional assay (platelet activation, specific); UFH (higher HIT risk) vs LMWH (lower risk but cross-reacts, so still avoided); argatroban (hepatobiliary clearance) vs bivalirudin (proteolytic and renal clearance).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the first action in a high-probability case (stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant, not LMWH), whether to test a low 4Ts score, which assay is most specific, argatroban’s half-life and APTT target, and why warfarin waits.

comparisons.title: PF4 immunoassay vs functional assay

right.label: Functional (SRA, HIPA)
points: Detects platelet activation by patient serum

comparisons.distinguisher: Antibody present vs antibody that activates platelets.

mnemonic.text: Stop EVERY DROP (infusions, flushes, coated lines), shun the COUSIN (LMWH), switch to a STRANGER (a non-heparin anticoagulant).
mnemonic.explanation: Encodes the three management steps of acute HIT.
mnemonic.limitation: Fondaparinux is heparin-like but is a guideline-suggested option because it only rarely causes HIT; warfarin is a non-heparin drug but must wait for platelet recovery; with a low 4Ts score, do not test or treat for HIT at all.

analogyLimitations: Assay performance figures vary by kit, threshold and laboratory.
takeaway: In suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, score the 4Ts first, test only intermediate or high scores with a sensitive immunoassay backed by a more specific functional assay, and treat by stopping every heparin source, including low-molecular-weight heparin, and switching to a non-heparin anticoagulant.

questions.stem: A patient on heparin with thrombocytopenia has a definite alternative cause, and the 4Ts score is 2 points. According to the ASH 2018 guideline, what is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: No HIT laboratory testing and no empiric HIT treatment; look for the other cause
options.rationale: Correct. A low 4Ts score (0–3 points) has a negative predictive value of about 99.8%; ASH recommends against testing and against empiric treatment.
Incorrect. Functional assays follow a positive immunoassay in intermediate- or high-probability patients.
Incorrect. Empiric HIT treatment is not recommended with a low-probability score.

options.text: Switch to low-molecular-weight heparin as a precaution
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is not a HIT strategy, and LMWH is avoided when HIT is likely.

questions.stem: Day 7 of unfractionated heparin: platelets fall 60% and a new DVT appears; the PF4 immunoassay is strongly positive. Which management is correct?

options.text: Stop all heparin, including flushes, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
options.rationale: Correct. Stop every heparin source and anticoagulate with a non-heparin drug at therapeutic intensity.

options.text: Switch to enoxaparin, a low-molecular-weight heparin
options.rationale: Incorrect. HIT antibodies react with LMWH; it is excluded in HIT.

options.text: Start warfarin immediately to cover the DVT
options.rationale: Incorrect. A vitamin K antagonist should not be started until the platelet count recovers.
Incorrect. Routine platelet transfusion is not suggested; it may be considered only with bleeding or high bleeding risk.

questions.stem: Which test is the more specific confirmation of HIT antibodies after a positive PF4 immunoassay?

options.text: A washed-platelet functional assay, such as the serotonin-release assay
options.rationale: Correct. Functional assays detect platelet-activating antibodies, and inhibition by high heparin concentrations adds specificity.
Incorrect. Immunoassays also detect antibodies that do not activate platelets, so they are the least specific test type; the guideline next step after a positive immunoassay is a functional assay.
Incorrect. The 4Ts score estimates pretest probability; it is not a confirmatory test.
Incorrect. The PT does not detect HIT antibodies.

claims.text: PF4/heparin antigen, IgG immune complexes, FcγIIa platelet activation, thrombosis risk; timing and rapid onset; UFH vs LMWH risk.
4Ts components, point bands, NPV ~99.8%, PPV ~14%/64%; no testing or empiric treatment for low scores; caveat about a score of 3.
EIA sensitivity >99% with lower specificity; IgG-specific more specific; functional assays more specific and used after a positive immunoassay; high-heparin inhibition.

Stop all heparin sources; avoid LMWH; non-heparin options; argatroban and bivalirudin half-lives, clearance and APTT target; argatroban raises INR; no VKA until platelet recovery; no routine platelet transfusion.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 39 Hit 2 (and the Number Vault) gives “low 4T score = 0–3% HIT probability”. In the sources, 0–3 is the point range of the low-probability category; its probability is given as <5% with a negative predictive value of about 99.8%, and HIT has been reported with a score of 3 (register flag rv-hit-4t-low-points).

Ch. 39 Hit 11 gives PF4-ELISA sensitivity ~98% and specificity ~89% as fixed values. Sources describe EIA sensitivity >99% and specificity that depends on the assay (IgG-specific vs polyspecific), threshold and clinical context, with reported ranges as low as 40–70% (register flag rv-hit-eia-specificity).

Ch. 39 Hit 2 states fondaparinux “does not cross-react in vivo”. Sources say fondaparinux is immunogenic but only rarely reported as a cause of HIT, call its risk negligible, and list it among conditional (very low certainty) options with danaparoid and DOACs (register flag rv-hit-fondaparinux-context).
